method: Host sizing begins with the virtual workload. The vCPUs to place are the VM count multiplied by the vCPUs per VM; dividing that total by the target vCPU-per-core ratio gives the physical cores the scheduler needs, and spreading those cores over whole hosts gives the CPU host count, each division rounded up because a cluster cannot hold a fractional host. Memory is counted separately as VM count multiplied by RAM per VM against the usable RAM on each host, again rounded up to whole hosts. The larger of the two host counts sizes the base cluster and is reported as the binding constraint, so a tie is shown as CPU and memory. Spare hosts kept for HA carry no workload: they are added after the base count, and because they still contribute cores and memory they raise the provisioned capacity without improving the achieved ratio. The achieved vCPU-per-core figure is the total vCPUs divided by every physical core in the sized cluster including spares, so it lands at or below the target once hosts are rounded up; average VMs per host spreads the VM count over all hosts; memory committed compares guest RAM with the memory of all hosts; and spare capacity is the remaining vCPUs at the target ratio together with the remaining RAM. Worked default: 120 VMs at 4 vCPUs each are 480 vCPUs, 480 divided by 4 is 120 physical cores, or 4 hosts of 32 cores, and 120 VMs at 16 GB are 1920 GB against 512 GB per host, also 4 hosts, so the cluster is 4 hosts plus 1 HA spare, 5 hosts of 160 cores, with a 3.0 achieved ratio and 1920 of 2560 GB committed. Limits: 1 to 10000 VMs, 1 to 64 vCPUs per VM, 1 to 256 cores per host, a vCPU-per-core target from 1 to 16, 0.25 to 1024 GB of RAM per VM, 1 to 8192 GB of usable RAM per host, and 0 to 8 HA spare hosts. A missing, malformed or out-of-range value is rejected with an actionable message rather than defaulted. The model assumes a uniform VM profile with no CPU reservations or limits, counts physical cores rather than hyperthreads, expects usable RAM to exclude the hypervisor reservation, and does not model NUMA layout, per-VM demand curves, storage or network bottlenecks, licensing, failure-domain placement or vendor sizing rules. Calculations run entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: vCPUs to place are the VM count times the vCPUs per VM; the physical cores required are that total divided by the target vCPU-per-core ratio, rounded up.
Hosts for CPU spread the required cores over whole hosts, while hosts for memory spread guest RAM over usable RAM per host; the larger count sizes the cluster and is the binding constraint.
HA spare hosts are added after the base count and carry no workload, so they add provisioned cores and memory without changing the workload ratio.
The achieved vCPU-per-core ratio is total vCPUs divided by all provisioned physical cores, and memory committed is guest RAM as a share of total host memory.
